title: Bean Et Al. - 2025 - Measuring What
chunk_summaries: The paper "Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks" is authored by a diverse group of researchers from institutions including the University of Oxford, EPFL, and Stanford University, among others. It focuses on the concept of construct validity in the evaluation of large language models (LLMs), emphasizing the importance of accurately measuring what these models are intended to assess. The authors argue for the need to refine benchmarks to ensure they effectively capture the capabilities and limitations of LLMs, thereby enhancing the reliability of their evaluations. The collaborative effort highlights the interdisciplinary nature of AI research and the collective aim to improve standards in LLM assessment.

The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is essential for understanding their capabilities and identifying safety and robustness issues before deployment. This requires strong construct validity to ensure that measures accurately reflect the phenomena being assessed. A systematic review conducted by a team of 29 expert reviewers analyzed 445 LLM benchmarks from prominent natural language processing and machine learning conferences. The review revealed patterns in the measured phenomena, tasks, and scoring metrics that compromise the validity of the claims made. To improve the situation, the authors offer eight key recommendations and actionable guidance for researchers and practitioners in the development of LLM benchmarks.

The development of large language models (LLMs) relies heavily on benchmarks and evaluations, which help assess model improvements and guide future research. Creating effective benchmarks involves translating abstract concepts into measurable tasks and metrics, a process that is crucial for establishing construct validity—the extent to which a benchmark accurately reflects the phenomenon it aims to measure. A systematic review of 445 articles from major ML and NLP conferences revealed that many benchmarks suffer from weaknesses in defining and operationalizing key concepts, leading to unreliable conclusions. The review emphasizes the need for shared standards and best practices to enhance construct validity, highlighting issues such as reproducibility and social responsibility. Recommendations for improving benchmark practices and an operational checklist for establishing construct validity are proposed to mitigate the risks of poorly supported scientific claims and misdirected research.

Construct validity assesses whether a test accurately measures the intended phenomenon, originating from psychological testing for unverifiable traits like personality. It encompasses various aspects, including face validity (the test's apparent validity), content validity (representation of all important aspects), ecological and predictive validity (real-world relevance and future performance prediction), and convergent, discriminant, and criterion validity (correlation with similar tests). In the context of large language models (LLMs), construct validity is essential for evaluating abstract abilities like reasoning, especially as standard benchmarks become saturated and focus shifts to general-purpose capabilities. The interpretation of these evaluations is debated, highlighting the importance of construct validity in determining signs of intelligence or emergent abilities in LLMs.

The study conducted a systematic review of 46,114 articles from major machine learning and natural language processing conferences between 2018 and 2024, focusing on those that mentioned 'benchmark' and either 'LLM' or 'language model.' This process yielded an initial set of 2,189 articles, which were filtered down to 522 using three criteria related to LLM capabilities, empirical benchmarks, and compatibility with text and vision models. A manual review by 29 experts further narrowed the selection to 445 articles. An a priori codebook was developed to assess key aspects of construct validity, and each article was coded by primary and secondary reviewers. The findings were synthesized into recommendations through an iterative process involving multiple authors.

The review process yielded a dataset of responses to 21 question items across 445 benchmark articles, annotated by 29 experts in NLP and machine learning. The dataset shows a significant increase in the number of articles published each year and covers various stages of benchmarks, including definitions of phenomena, task selection, and performance metrics for language models. The reviewed benchmarks encompass a wide range of phenomena, with 78.2% providing definitions, though 47.8% of these definitions are contested. Tasks varied widely, with less than 10% using complete real-world tasks, while 40.7% employed constructed tasks. The methodology for selecting task items significantly impacts benchmark validity, with 55.2% using partially targeted sampling. The most common response format was free response, and the primary scoring metric was exact matching, used by 81.3% of benchmarks. Additionally, 53.4% of articles provided evidence for their benchmark's construct validity, with many comparing their results to other benchmarks or human baselines.

The text outlines five recommendations aimed at enhancing the construct validity of large language model (LLM) benchmarks. It emphasizes the importance of broadly applicable suggestions, acknowledging that not all recommendations will be relevant to every benchmark. Each recommendation is accompanied by a specific checklist of items to consider when developing a new benchmark.

To effectively measure a phenomenon, it is essential to provide a precise and operational definition, specify its scope, and acknowledge any excluded aspects. A clear definition aids in understanding and operationalizing the concept, as evidenced by 78.2% of reviewed benchmarks that include definitions. In cases where multiple definitions exist, selecting one can clarify the benchmark's intent, while a negative definition can help establish boundaries when consensus is lacking, as seen in 47.8% of benchmarks. Additionally, if the phenomenon has sub-components, measuring them separately, as done in 61.2% of benchmarks, enhances clarity and interpretation, although combining measures can be beneficial when no single measure suffices.

To accurately measure a phenomenon, it is essential to control for unrelated tasks that may influence results and assess the impact of format constraints on model performance. Benchmark tasks often involve both specific and general abilities, with unmeasured subtasks potentially confounding the measurement. For instance, 21.1% of benchmarks require specific output formats that can challenge models, while complex instructions may disproportionately affect weaker models. Strategies to mitigate these confounding effects include establishing baselines for relevant subtasks, testing models on world knowledge separately, and validating automated output parsing techniques to avoid biases. Additionally, factor analysis techniques are being explored to identify latent capabilities with minimal interference from auxiliary tasks.

To construct a representative dataset for evaluating tasks, it is essential to employ effective sampling strategies that reflect the overall task space, particularly for large or automatically generated datasets. Quality and relevance of task items must be verified, and items should include variations that test known sensitivities of large language models (LLMs). Many benchmarks currently rely on convenience sampling, which can lead to non-representative results, as seen in examples like the AIME exam questions that favor basic arithmetic. It is recommended that authors utilize more robust sampling methods, such as random or stratified sampling, to enhance construct validity and reduce computational costs. Additionally, care should be taken when generating synthetic examples to avoid non-representative sampling, and task items should be designed to address common LLM weaknesses, such as sensitivity to prompt variations.

The text emphasizes the importance of acknowledging the limitations associated with reusing datasets in benchmarking. It advises documenting whether a benchmark adapts a previous dataset, analyzing the strengths and weaknesses of the adapted work, and comparing performance against the original. With 38.2% of reviewed benchmarks reusing data, this practice complicates the control of construct validity and restricts design choices, while also increasing the risk of benchmarking tasks overlapping with pre-training data. Newly constructed datasets are preferred, but if reuse occurs (as in 7.7% of cases), authors should investigate and document changes made, justifying differences between original and new datasets. Reporting these differences is crucial for demonstrating the impact of modifications on construct validity.

To prepare for data contamination in benchmarks, it is essential to implement tests for detecting contamination and maintain a held-out set of task items for ongoing evaluation. Investigating the pre-exposure of benchmark source materials in common LLM training corpora is also crucial. The process by which an LLM arrives at an answer is important, as contamination can arise from direct exposure to benchmark items or memorization of related information, potentially undermining result validity. To mitigate this, it is recommended to vet test items for contamination during benchmark creation, especially for public datasets or when LLMs generate task examples. Incorporating contamination checks within the benchmark can ensure ongoing validity, and dynamic benchmarks or procedurally generated tasks may help keep benchmarks current.

To effectively compare models, it is essential to employ statistical methods in benchmarking, including reporting sample size and justifying statistical power, as well as providing uncertainty estimates for primary scores. When using human raters, their demographics should be described, and potential biases in recruitment and instructions should be addressed. Metrics should reflect the inherent variability of subjective labels rather than relying on single-point aggregation. Currently, only 16.0% of reviewed benchmarks utilize statistical testing, highlighting the need for more robust methods in LLM benchmarking. Additionally, the aggregation of ratings should consider the distribution and representativeness of raters, especially in contexts involving bias and harm, to ensure that results are relevant for real-world applications.

The text outlines the process of conducting an error analysis and justifying construct validity for benchmarks in evaluating models. It emphasizes the importance of both qualitative and quantitative analyses of failure modes to identify scoring biases and improve construct validity. A well-validated benchmark should correlate errors with the intended phenomenon rather than confounders. The GSM8K benchmark is used as a practical example, highlighting its definition, operationalization, and the need for clear task metrics. Recommendations include addressing confounders, constructing a representative dataset, acknowledging limitations, and conducting error analyses to enhance reliability. The conclusion notes that while GSM8K is a valid benchmark for grade school math, issues like contamination and the lack of error analysis could be improved for better interpretability.

A systematic review of 445 benchmarks in NLP and ML literature identified significant gaps in construct validity, with many benchmarks lacking clear definitions, appropriate task adjustments, and statistical testing. Although about half of the reviewed articles addressed validity, most had weaknesses in at least one area. The authors proposed eight recommendations and created a practical operational checklist to guide researchers in enhancing construct validity throughout the benchmark lifecycle, from design to interpretation. This checklist aids in task selection and metric justification and can also evaluate existing benchmarks. The review, which assessed 2,189 papers and achieved a precision of about 85%, highlighted the importance of clear definitions and reliable coding processes, with inter-rater agreement showing moderate consistency. Limitations include potential exclusion of impactful benchmarks and risks of undetected errors from automated screening. The authors call for a cultural shift in the research community to prioritize construct validity for meaningful evaluation of large language models (LLMs).

Ultimately, the authors call for a cultural shift in the research community to prioritize construct validity for a meaningful evaluation of LLMs, reinforcing the need for clear definitions and reliable coding processes, as well as addressing the limitations of automated screening that may overlook impactful benchmarks.
